The petitioner claims to be the owner of Plot
 Nos.793/981 and 791/982 within Mouza -
 Kashinagar, Jl No.9 under Police Station - Kakdwip
 in the District of South 24-Parganas measuring an
 area of about 0.16 acres and 0.21 acres respectively.

A proceeding being Case No.LA-II/40 of 1983-84
 under the West Bengal Land (Requisition and
 Acquisition) Act, 1948 (for short, Act Ii of 1948) was
 initiated for the purpose of construction of approach
 road to dril site for Project Manager Ongc.

sentences.text: The possession of the lands in  question
was taken on March 13, 1984.
2  The petitioner alleges that no notice under Section 4(1a) of Act II of 1948 was published in the Official Gazette.

Mr. Pan, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that in the meantime Act II of 1948 expired and no step was taken by the State respondent to acquire the said property by resorting to the provisions of Section 9(3A) or 9(3B), as the case may be.
Mr. Pan submits that the property of the petitioner has been utilized for the aforesaid purpose but no compensation has been paid to the petitioner till date.
Mr. Mahato, learned Advocate appearing for the State submits that the writ petitioner has approached this court at a belated stage as the writ petition was filed only in the month of December, 2011.
He further submits that ad hoc compensation amounting to 80% of the land value has been paid to the recorded owner of the said land.
Mr. Mahato further submits that the name of the petitioner was not recorded in the record of rights and, therefore, he cannot claim compensation in respect of the aforesaid lands.

In reply, Mr. Pan, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner placed reliance upon a decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh and Others reported at (2020) 2 SCC 569 in support of his contention that delay and laches cannot be raised in a case of a continuing cause of action.
Heard the learned Advocates for the parties and perused the materials placed.

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Vidya Devi (supra) took note of the decision in the case of Tukaram Kana Joshi v. MIDC reported at (2013) 1 SCC 353 wherein it was observed that there are authorities which state that delay and laches extinguish the right to put forth a claim.

entities.text: Tukaram Kana Joshi v. MIDC reported at (2013) 1 SCC 353
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Most of these authorities pertain to service jurisprudence, grant of compensation for a wrong done to them decades ago, recovery of statutory dues, claim for educational facilities and other categories of similar cases, etc.

It was further observed that though it is true that there are a few authorities that lay down that delay and laches debar a citizen from seeking remedy, even if his fundamental right has been violated, under Article 32 or 226 of the Constitution, the case at hand deals with a different scenario altogether.
It was held therein that in the said reported case the functionaries of the State took over possession of the land belonging to the appellants without any sanction of law.
The appellants had asked repeatedly for grant of the benefit of compensation.
The State must either comply with the procedure laid down for acquisition, or requisition, or any other permissible statutory mode.

After taking note of the said decision, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that delay and laches cannot be raised in a case of a continuing cause of action, or if the circumstances shock the judicial conscience of the court.
Condonation of delay is a matter of judicial discretion, which must be exercised judiciously and reasonably in the facts and circumstances of a case.
It will depend upon the breach of fundamental rights, and the remedy claimed, and when and how the delay arose.

There is no period of limitation prescribed for the courts to exercise their constitutional jurisdiction to do substantial justice and in a case where the demand for justice is so compelling, a constitutional court would exercise its jurisdiction with a view to promote justice and not defeat it.
In the case on hand, a proceeding for requisition was initiated by issuing an order passed under Section 3 of Act II of 1948.
Possession was taken as far back as in the month of March, 1984.
The authorities for reasons best known to them, did not publish notice under Section 4(1a) of Act II of 1948 during the lifetime of Act II of 1948 for acquiring the said property.
In the meantime, Act II of 1948 stood expired.
The State has filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein it has been admitted that the petitioner is the owner of Plot Nos.793/981 and 791/982 for area of about 0.16 acres and 0.21 acres respectively.
An entry in the record of rights neither creates any title nor does it extinguish any right.
In view of the admission made by the State in its affidavit, the alleged non-recording of the name of the petitioner in the record of rights is of no relevance.

It has been further stated in the said affidavit that as the proceeding of land acquisition could not be completed before March, 1997, the proceeding for land acquisition may be completed under Section 9(3A) or 9(3B) of the Amendment Act of 1997.

In the meantime, the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 stood repealed with the coming into force of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (for short "the 2013 Act") which came into force with effect from 1st January, 2014.

sentences.text: It is not in dispute that the land has been utilized for the purpose for which the same was requisitioned.
The order of requisition passed under Section 3(1) could not have been extended after the lifetime of Act II of 1948.
The possession of the land in question after expiry of Act II of 1948 without taking any steps for acquiring the same amounts to gross abuse of the powers of the State.

The State is retaining its possession of the lands in question without paying compensation to the petitioner in accordance with the provisions of the relevant statute.
Though the possession of the land was taken in exercise of the power of requisition under Act II of 1948, retention of possession for an indefinite period without payment of adequate compensation is without any sanction of law.
Such an action shocks the conscience of this court.
Payment of an amount of 80% of the estimated land value cannot be said to be an adequate compensation.
Such payment does not entitle the State to retain possession of land requisitioned for an indefinite period.
Such payment cannot be a substitute for payment of compensation in terms of an Award made under the relevant statute.
For such reason, this court is inclined to exercise discretion in favour of the petitioner as the demand for justice is very compelling.
Such discretion is being exercised by this court with a view to promote justice.
State cannot deprive a citizen of his property without paying compensation in accordance with the relevant statute.

At this stage, it would be relevant to take note of the decision of the Hon'ble Division Bench in the case of State of West Bengal & Others v. Ganesh Samanta reported at (2014) 4 WBLR (Cal) 996 wherein the Hon'ble Division Bench after noting the decision of the Special Bench in the case of State of West Bengal & Others v. Sabita Mondal reported at (2011) 3 CHN (Cal) 555 observed that the State Government could have completed the acquisition proceedings by completing the provision contained in Section 9(3A) of the Land Acquisition Act but in view of the subsequent development in the Land Acquisition Laws with the enactment of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 and particularly in view of Section 24(1)(a) of the said Act the State could not have completed the acquisition proceeding by following Section 9(3A) of the Land Acquisition Act, which has since been repealed.

sentences.text: After noting the aforesaid provisions, the Hon'ble Division Bench held that the State respondents are required to complete the acquisition proceeding by following the relevant provision of the 2013 Act.

This court was inclined to pass an order by applying the proposition of law laid down in Ganesh Samanta (supra).
At this stage, Mr. Mahato, learned Advocate appearing for the State submits that the petitioner can consider the proposal of the State for direct purchase of the land in question.

sentences.text: In reply to such suggestion of Mr. Mahato, Mr. Pan, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that if a concrete proposal from a responsible officer of the State Government comes to the petitioner with regard to the purchase of land directly from the petitioner in accordance with the Direct Land Policy contained in Memorandum No.756-LP/1A- 03/14(Pt.II) dated February 25, 2016, the petitioner shall consider the same.
Mr. Mahato, learned Advocate for the State prays for some time to file an affidavit by a responsible officer of the State in that regard.

As prayed for by Mr. Mahato, learned Advocate, the Special Land Acquisition Officer, South 24-Parganas, being the 3rd respondent, shall file an affidavit stating as to whether the State is agreeable to purchase the land directly from the petitioner in terms of the aforesaid Memo and shall also specifically state in the said affidavit the time within which the entire process shall be concluded.
Let such affidavit be filed on or before December 20, 2024.
List this matter on December 23, 2024 under the heading "For Orders".

(HIRANMAY BHATTACHARYYA, J.)
